title: Sit in your cell
hookLine: a desert father's advice: sit in your cell and your cell will teach you everything

cards: A brother has crossed the desert to Scetis to see an old monk called Abba Moses. He asks what visitors to the desert asked: give me a word, one saying to live by. Perhaps he expects something hard.
The old man answers with one sentence. Go, sit in your cell, and your cell will teach you everything. That's all.
No program. No follow-up. A word that sounds too simple to work.

teach.b: Start with the title. The visitor calls him abba. It's the word for father, and Christians knew it from the Gospel: in Gethsemane, in Mark's telling, Jesus prays, "Abba, Father."
In the desert, abba became the name for an elder whose life gave his words weight. Those short sayings were gathered into the collection we call the Sayings of the Desert Fathers. Next, the man.

Tradition says Abba Moses had a rough past before he became a monk, and the sayings remember him for humility. Once, they say, the brothers called a meeting to judge a monk who had sinned. Moses at first refused to come.

When they sent for him again, he came carrying a leaking jug of water. Asked why, he said his own sins were running out behind him where he couldn't see them, and here he was, coming to judge someone else's.
The brothers said no more, and forgave the one who had sinned. Third, the cell. A monk's cell wasn't a prison.

teach.h: A CELL IS A SMALL ROOM.
teach.b: It was his small hut or room, where he prayed, slept and worked. So why would a room teach everything? Some readers hear it this way: when you stop going elsewhere, you meet what you brought with you.
Restlessness. Boredom. The itch to check on something, anything.
The urge to leave. On that reading, those aren't distractions from the lesson. They are the lesson.
Staying put, the sayings suggest, lets you see yourself without the usual escape routes, and that's where prayer starts to get honest.
Fourth, your own cell: a kitchen, a bedroom, a parked car, a desk at lunch.

how: Catholic monks and nuns keep times of silence in their cells and cloisters, and many lay Catholics set aside a quiet place at home for prayer.

the head bishop over the churches of Egypt
father: a title for a wise elder of the desert

games.q: you've crossed the desert to Scetis and asked Abba Moses for a word to live by. what does he tell you?
o: fast and pray through the night.
go, sit in your cell, and your cell will teach you everything.
visit every elder in the desert.
games.why: one sentence. no program, no rule: stay in your room, and let staying put do the teaching.

practice: Wherever you are, that's your cell: don't get up, don't tidy, don't reach for the phone. Notice what wants to leave first, your hands, your eyes, your thoughts, and just stay.
If you pray, say the two words from Gethsemane, Abba, Father, and let the rest be quiet; if not, let your breath be the only thing that moves.

wordCard.voice: Abba. Father: the word Jesus prays in Gethsemane, and the name the desert gave its elders. Today's word.

orig.note: father — an Aramaic word kept in Mark's Greek Gospel, and the desert's title for an elder.

carryVoice: Your line: the cell teaches. Even a small room can be enough, if you stay. Until tomorrow.
